Although the digest separates the renderings into three "senses," phrases like "causes sin than" and "than hell" are really fragments of surrounding sentences rather than distinct meanings of the word, which consistently denotes hell.
prose.caution: The listed "senses" beyond "hell" reflect how surrounding words were captured rather than genuinely different meanings, so γέεννα effectively carries a single sense.

receipts.how: Jesus calls scribes and Pharisees 'sons of hell,' demonstrating γέεννα as the place of final punishment, the core sense the definition captures.
Jesus warns to fear the one who can throw into hell, confirming the word's consistent use as a noun denoting a place of punishment across non-Matthean authors.
James describes the tongue as 'set on fire by hell,' showing the word retains its meaning as a place of fiery judgment even in metaphorical use outside the Synoptics.

audit.author_note: Matthew uses γέεννα 7 of 12 times, almost always on the lips of Jesus in ethical warnings; James uses it once in a vivid metaphor about the tongue, suggesting a slightly more figurative rhetorical application, though the underlying denotation remains the same place of fiery judgment.
